title: Nuclear, Astrophysics & Practical Skills — Final Depth Practice
subject: physics

questions.prompt: In alpha decay, the nucleus emits:
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — an alpha particle is ⁴₂He: 2 protons and 2 neutrons.
questions.feedbackWrong: Alpha is a helium-4 nucleus. Electrons are beta-minus; photons are gamma; neutrons are released in fission or beta-plus processes, not alpha.

mistakes.correction: Beta is an electron emitted when a neutron converts to a proton; alpha is the heavy helium nucleus — mass number drops by 4 in alpha, unchanged in beta.

questions.prompt: A radioactive sample has activity 800 Bq. After 24 hours the activity is 50 Bq. Enter the half-life in hours.
A star like the Sun will end its life as:
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — low-mass stars shed their outer layers as planetary nebulae, leaving white dwarf cores.
questions.feedbackWrong: Only high-mass stars (roughly above 8 solar masses) end as neutron stars or black holes — the Sun's remnant is a white dwarf.

mistakes.misconception: Assumes all stars die in supernovae.
mistakes.correction: Supernovae require high mass. Sun-like stars pass through red giant and planetary nebula stages to a quietly cooling white dwarf.

questions.prompt: A galaxy's light is redshifted, indicating recessional velocity 2100 km/s. Taking H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc, enter the galaxy's distance in Mpc.

A student measures a wire's diameter as 0.52 mm ± 0.01 mm and its length as 1.500 m ± 0.001 m. Explain which measurement contributes more uncertainty to the calculated cross-sectional area, and why the diameter matters especially much.

markScheme.text: Percentage uncertainty in diameter ≈ 0.01/0.52 ≈ 2%; in length ≈ 0.07%.
Diameter uncertainty dominates — it is far larger in percentage terms.
Area depends on d², so the diameter's percentage uncertainty doubles to ≈ 4%.
Conclusion: improving the diameter measurement (micrometer, repeated readings) reduces uncertainty most effectively.

questions.prompt: A thermometer consistently reads 2°C too high in every measurement. This is:
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — a consistent offset in one direction is systematic; repeating measurements cannot average it away.
questions.feedbackWrong: Systematic errors shift all readings the same way — only recalibration fixes them. Random errors scatter both directions and reduce with repeats.

mistakes.misconception: Assumes any offset must be a zero error.
mistakes.correction: Zero error is one cause of systematic error, but a constant offset can also come from calibration drift or incorrect scaling — the category is systematic.

questions.prompt: Explain why energy is released in nuclear fission, using the binding energy per nucleon curve.

markScheme.text: Heavy nuclei like uranium sit on the falling part of the curve beyond iron.
Fission products have higher binding energy per nucleon than the parent nucleus.
The difference in total binding energy corresponds to mass converted to energy via E = mc².
